The Audacity Era: Kayla Nicole on Doing the Scary Thing Anyway

Kayla Nicole began training in gymnastics at only 5 years old. What started as fun and playful sessions quickly developed into a disciplined regimen of focus. She learned all about the type of commitment it takes to become a competitive athlete by focusing on diet, exercise, and training. She used that early dedication to carry herself through Pepperdine University’s prestigious broadcast journalism degree program and into a massive media career that spans genres. Her early media icons were leading ladies in everyone’s favorite romcoms, including the Toni Braxton, with whom she had a chance to perform. These moments aren’t serendipitous; they are the culmination of Kayla’s incredible use of social media to show people her personality and well of talent. Kayla always knew that she belonged in front of the camera, helping people tell their stories. She got practice in both, working in retail and modeling in L.A. During this episode of Naked Beauty she talked all about her incredible discipline and how it informs everything from her daily workouts to her pursuit of media success. They also chat about what it was like growing up in a family of women, headed by a glamorous matriarch who believes in self-care. They discuss the alluring red carpet events and how support from a therapist helped her surmount a season of depression. The conversation is candid and funny, and it mirrors the Kayla Nicole her audience has grown to love.

title: “I Would Move To Another Country”: Callum Turner & Monica Barbaro On One Night Only’s Absurd No Sex Mandate Premise
text:
“I Would Move To Another Country”: Callum Turner & Monica Barbaro On One Night Only’s Absurd No Sex Mandate Premise

When the trailer for One Night Only, Will Gluck’s new rom-com starring Monica Barbaro and Callum Turner, dropped, its absurd premise ignited a firestorm of debate across social media. In the movie, Allie (Barbaro) and Owen (Turner) play “two strangers [who] crash into each other in an ever-so-slightly fictionalized New York on the one night when single people are allowed to have sex,” as the official logline reads. The questions were immediate: How is the mandate enforced? What counts as sex in this sexless world? Why? How? What? The movie answers all of these questions (some more comprehensively than others) but the point is: One Night Only is a romantic comedy, emphasis on comedy. It’s supposed to be absurd. It’s supposed to make you laugh at the caricature portrayals of politicians who would enforce such archaic, puritanical beliefs. It’s close enough to reality — incels and tradwives alike are already pushing the anti-hookup culture agenda — that the jokes land. The premise is also just a purposely ludicrous backdrop to the love story. 

And Barbaro and Turner are so delightfully charming together that as you’re watching the film, the logistics and terrifyingly fascist implications of the aforementioned premise fade away and it becomes a fun, adventurous, flirtatious romp between two young, hot, horny singles. Try not to overthink it. When Refinery29 talked to the One Night Only stars in New York City before the film’s release, Barbaro and Turner were playful and at ease with each other, slipping easily into banter mirroring that of their characters, Allie and Owen. As Allie, Barbaro is engaging, slightly neurotic and relatably confident in one moment and insecure the next. As Owen, Turner is a solid leading man, delivering impeccable longing looks and yearning glances while also playing the faux bravado of a young man on the prowl perfectly. Together, they are a joy to watch. The pair are often in headlines for their dating lives (Turner just married mega pop star Dua Lipa and Barbaro is reportedly dating fellow actor Andrew Garfield), but their talent should stand on its own. They are both formidable romance leads. Here, the stars defend the movie’s controversial premise, make a case for getting serenaded on a date, and rattle off each other’s coffee and pizza orders without hesitation. 

The premise is so wild, but the movie grounds it in reality. There are —  terrifyingly — moments where I was like, “Oh, this could actually happen.” There’s a reference to incels, and as some of the politicians are speaking, it makes you think, “Wow, we’re maybe not too far off.” So, if this did happen in real life, how do you think it would go down?

Monica Barbaro: I think parts of this movie feel pretty familiar. I think it would feel like this really high-stress thing where everyone feels like they have to make the most of this one night, and maybe along the way forget about the more important deeper connections that can also [happen].

Callum Turner: The night’s kind of like New Year’s Eve, Halloween, Valentine’s Day, 4th of July, wrapped into one. 

MB: Chaos.

CT: It’s chaos. 

MB: And it’s that thing where, I feel like every New Year’s, I want to do something really nice, or Halloween, I’m like, I’m going to wear this, I’m going to do this costume, and I’m going to make it really fun. That happens in like early September, and then by the time it’s October 28th, I’m like, “Oh, shit. I have to find something in my drawer.” I would never be able to plan out my One Night Only well and then inevitably be disappointed. 

The movie sets up the disappointment, but it also sets up this anticipation and the buildup, and desperation that would come with a premise like this. One of the back and forths that I love between your characters is debating whether the buildup or the after is the best part of sex. Who are you with in that argument? 

CT: I think they’ve both got points. 

MB: I think they both have a solid case [laughs]. There are 365 days of the year, we’d be absolutely fine. Humans would be fine.

CT: As celibate?

MB: [laughs] I’m just saying the build up and the after both are great [but] I don’t believe in this mandate. I don’t think it should happen. Nobody accuse me of that, please. I would move to another country! 

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Refinery29 (@refinery29)

There are two different instances where Allie is being sung to on a date. In one, she is charmed by it. And in the other, she gets the ick. Do you think there’s ever an okay time to be sung to on a date?

MB: I think there’s always an okay time to be sung to. I think it’s more the lyrics of that particular song. 

CT: The first song you’re singing with him, too, right? 

MB: Yeah. He sings first and it’s lovely, and she sings along. One of my favorite lines in this whole movie is, “It’s not a duet.” It’s one of my favorite moments.

So, you’re all for being serenaded? 

MB: Yeah, it’s just that then if you turn the lyrics to something that I won’t say, that’s the end of that. 

CT: Now I have the lyrics in my head. 

MB: He has this thing where if you say a song, he has to start singing it. See, he’s sweating. 

CT: That one I’m not going to do. 

MB: We have to get a new song in his head. Um, Stand By Me! [laughs]

CT: I’m not going to do it. 

In the movie, it’s said that you don’t know somebody unless you know their pizza and their coffee orders. So, what are your pizza and coffee orders? 

CT: [Monica’s is] Cortado, oat milk. Margarita pizza, but if she’s feeling a little crazy, then she’ll throw everything on there. 

MB: Callum’s is a cappuccino, margarita pizza. 

CT: Oh, we know! 

MB: We said it like we’re really sad [but] we just locked in [laughs].

If you haven’t been keeping up on rom-coms, romance is back in a big way on TV and on film. Why do you think it left for a while and why do you think it’s back?

MB: I definitely think right now people need that catharsis. It’s kind of a wild time and even just like people trying to date in a big city, I think this movie feels cathartic for at least like friends of mine because I think they can see themselves in Allie and see that experience, like see those moments in dating where suddenly, “Oh, this turned. I got to get out of here.” Um and I think it’s just so fun to watch because of that. 

CT: And people love love. People love love! And watching people fall in love. And that’s what they get to do in this film.

One Night Only is in theaters now.

title: The Spider-Man: Brand New Day Kiss Everyone’s Talking About Is A Lesson In Consent
text:
The Spider-Man: Brand New Day Kiss Everyone’s Talking About Is A Lesson In Consent

Spoilers ahead. There’s a moment in Spider-Man: Brand New Day where Peter Parker (Tom Holland) finally gets MJ (Zendaya) back… or so he thinks. After saving her from Jean Grey’s (Sadie Sink) clutches, MJ appears to remember who he is, and the pair share a loving kiss. Soon, it’s revealed that Jean is in MJ’s mind, and Peter’s ex still has no memory of him.

When Peter is eventually reunited with the real MJ, he apologizes and admits to kissing her while she wasn’t present. Although MJ has no memory of this, fans have latched onto how Peter’s apology is a good depiction of consent. For a superhero movie to break down stereotypes of toxic masculinity and show a character like Peter Parker embracing emotions and genuinely being a good guy, it’s somewhat refreshing.

Angelique Wan, co-founder and CEO of Consent Labs, tells Refinery29 the reason it’s resonated with so many people is that it feels familiar to many people. “The scene reflects the reality that harm is not always obvious or intentional, and that conversations about consent are rarely black and white. People don’t always have all the information they need to make fully informed choices,” she says.

Peter and MJ aren’t presented as ‘heroes’ or ‘villains’ in this kiss situation, because it’s a grey area. “These nuanced, everyday scenarios make the scene so relatable and open the door to meaningful conversations about consent. It’s also worth noting that the film doesn’t extend the same nuance to Jean Grey, who acted with full knowledge of the situation,” Wan adds.

On Threads, people have praised Spider-Man: Brand New Day for including the scene where Peter apologized to MJ. At no point does he dismiss or minimize her experience, and instead, he takes responsibility. “[This] reinforces that consent is ongoing and dynamic. Just because Peter and MJ were previously in a relationship doesn’t mean consent can be assumed,” Wan explains. “The wider storyline also highlights that consent depends on informed choice, reminding us that deception or withholding important information can undermine someone’s ability to give affirmative consent.”

The expert tells R29 that stories like this on the big screen (especially ones as popular as this) can demonstrate what accountability looks like in practice. Peter’s acknowledgment that his actions could have hurt someone else, regardless of intention, sends an important message about owning your mistakes. “By centring the experiences of those affected by our actions, we can take accountability and practice relational skills that cultivate healthier relationships,” she says. “It also encourages people to speak up when something doesn’t feel right and to think about how their own actions can affect others.”

While Spider-Man is fiction, the real-world lessons it teaches young people are very real. Whether it’s about consent, respect, or healthy communication, it helps start a conversation and makes the tough conversations less awkward.

title: Copenhagen’s Wacky Shoe Trend Is All About The Big Toe
text:
Copenhagen’s Wacky Shoe Trend Is All About The Big Toe

Copenhagen Fashion Week has unofficially commenced the Fashion Month season with Spring/Summer 2027 collections and lots of striking street style. From elevated chain headwear and cargo Bermuda shorts to layered, undone hairstyles, there are tons of style ideas to take from the showgoers.

But the one viral style currently on everyone’s lips (likely on wide-eyed, jaw-dropped faces) is the new Havaianas kitten heel flip-flops, notably with big-toe caps. After being teased on the Brazilian brand’s socials, the statement sandals debuted on the Studio Constance runway on August 4. But because every brand makes heeled flip flops now, it seems that Havaianas really wanted to stand out from the rest, hence the not-so-typical concealed big toe design.

The wacky shoe of the moment is constantly evolving, from Maison Margiela’s split-toe Tabi flat revival to Tory Burch’s metal-pierced mules to Vibram’s FiveFinger utilitarian shoes. And somehow, someway, Copenhagen’s fashion It-girls are already wearing styles similar to the viral Havaianas. (Plus, just before writing this, I spotted toe-covered flip flops on the NYC subway.)

The Copenhagen street style outfits have predominantly consisted of trendy toe-ring sandals, unique peep-toe heels, and woven-fabric flats that each give peeks of summer pedicures. So maybe the solution to transitional-weather dressing — whether it’s from the summer into the fall or the winter into the spring — is not a standard flip flop or boot, but rather keeping a toe or two covered.

And wouldn’t you know it… even before Collina Strada’s Copenhagen debut on August 6, which had models strutting in cut-out toe socks in place of shoes, many runway attendees have already been pairing similar socks with their thong sandals or Havaianas flip flops. So, if the toe-cap styles are too avant-garde for you, consider DIYing socks into a faux leg-warmer look for the changing weather.  

Since the Havaianas heels aren’t available to purchase yet, shop alternatives for big-toe covered shoes, from funky cut-out heels and toe-ring sandals to strappy mules in the meantime.

title: Laser Hair Removal Changed My Confidence, But Finding The Right Place Took Years.
text:
Laser Hair Removal Changed My Confidence, But Finding The Right Place Took Years.

After being burned during a laser hair removal appointment years ago, I thought I’d never go back. Not only did the experience leave me physically scarred, but it also made me question whether laser clinics truly understood how to safely treat melanated skin. So, for years my relationship with laser hair removal was inconsistent at best — until I recently went to Milan Laser and finally experienced what laser hair removal should actually feel like. 

Why I Did It 

For years, I thought ingrown hairs were just something I had to deal with. Shaving constantly irritated my skin, waxing was painful, and no matter what I tried, I kept dealing with bumps and hyperpigmentation. By 2015, laser hair removal started feeling less like a luxury and more like a necessity. 

At the time, everyone was talking about the benefits of laser hair removal. Smoother skin, less irritation, and freedom from razor bumps. I was tired of feeling uncomfortable in my own skin, so I finally decided to try it. 

What Scared Me 

My first laser experience almost scared me away from the treatment completely. 

During an underarm session years ago, a technician accidentally burned part of my tattoo because she never asked if I had one or covered it before starting. I still have the scar today. After that, I became extremely hesitant about laser hair removal, especially because I wasn’t sure if many places truly understood how to safely treat melanated skin. 

Even though I saw some results over the years, the hair always seemed to grow back eventually. So, for nearly a decade, my relationship with laser hair removal became very on-and-off. I never found a place that made me feel fully comfortable or confident. 

The Laser Type 

Everything shifted when I went to Milan Laser Hair Removal. The moment my Black technician walked into the room, I instantly felt more at ease. I literally told her, “You don’t know how happy I am to see you,” and she smiled and said, “I’m happy to see you too.” 

It may sound small, but as a Black woman, there’s comfort in knowing someone understands your skin and your concerns. Before we even started, she asked detailed questions about my skin history, past laser experiences, and sensitivities. Nothing felt rushed. 

What also made me feel safer was learning that Milan’s technicians are licensed medical professionals and that they use the Candela GentleMax Pro laser, which is designed to safely treat a variety of skin tones, including melanated skin. 

What It Felt Like 

If you’ve never had laser hair removal before, the sensation feels like quick snaps against your skin with bursts of heat. It’s not exactly painless, but it’s far more tolerable than waxing in my opinion. 

What made the experience better at Milan was how thorough and attentive the technician was throughout the appointment. She constantly checked in to make sure I was comfortable and carefully treated every section instead of rushing through the process. The level of care honestly changed my perspective on laser hair removal. 

The Aftermath 

The results have been some of the best I’ve ever experienced. I’ve now gone back a few times, and the difference has honestly shocked me. My hair growth has slowed down significantly, my skin feels smoother, and I’m seeing far fewer ingrown hairs and dark marks. I haven’t had a session in over two months and barely see any regrowth. 

What I’d Tell A Friend 

I’d tell any friend considering laser hair removal to really do their research and find a place that understands melanated skin. That matters more than people realize. 

I’d also tell them not to settle for a rushed experience just because laser has become more common. You should feel comfortable asking questions, discussing concerns, and making sure the provider is educated on your skin specifically. And honestly? Seeing representation in these spaces matters too. 

The Cost 

One thing I appreciated about Milan Laser is their unlimited treatment model. Instead of paying for individual sessions over and over again, you pay once and can continue treatments as needed. Depending on the areas you treat, the price can range anywhere from $3,000-7,000.  

Considering how inconsistent my past experiences were, I think the investment is worth it. They also have more than 400 locations across 38 states, which makes it easy to continue treatments while traveling. 

The Verdict 

For years, laser hair removal felt intimidating to me because of my past experiences and concerns about whether providers truly understood Black skin. But this experience completely changed my perspective. The confidence boost goes beyond just being hair-free. It’s the relief of not constantly worrying about ingrown hairs, irritation, or hyperpigmentation. It’s feeling comfortable in sleeveless tops again. It’s not having to think about shaving before every trip or event. For the first time in a long time, laser hair removal finally feels worth it. 

Worth it. If you’ve ever dealt with ingrown hair, hyperpigmentation, or constantly having to think about shaving before every trip, event, or beach day, you get it. For me, laser hair was about feeling comfortable in my skin. The results have been some of the best I’ve seen in years, with significantly less hair growth, fewer ingrown hairs, and smoother skin overall. Add in the fact that I can continue treatments without worrying about paying for individual sessions, and it’s easily the best laser experience I’ve had to date. 

Skip it if you’re looking for instant gratification. Laser hair removal is a process, not a quick fix. You’ll need multiple sessions, and the results happen over time. But if you’re tired of dealing with razor bumps, ingrown hairs, and dark marks, and you’re willing to stick with it, it’s one of the best beauty investments I’ve made for myself.

title: Everyone’s Obsessed With Tretinoin — But I Don’t Have A Prescription
text:
Everyone’s Obsessed With Tretinoin — But I Don’t Have A Prescription

With 38.1K posts waxing lyrical about the topical skincare medication on TikTok, there’s simply no escaping it: Tretinoin is a skincare sensation. And with each scroll, we bet you’re asking yourself, Should I get in on the hype? 

You can’t just go out and buy tretinoin; you need a prescription from a dermatologist. That said, if you’ve recently come across tretinoin online, you can infer that it’s more widely prescribed today than ever before. “I’ve been prescribing it for 15 years,” says NYC-based dermatologist Michelle Henry, MD, “but there’s been a constant uptick in interest as people have become more educated about it.”

Similar to a skincare medication like Accutane or spironolactone, tretinoin requires a doctor to write you a pharmacy prescription and teach you how to use it safely and accurately. But unlike Accutane or spironolactone (a diuretic used to treat chronic hormonal acne), tretinoin is not an acne-specific medication. It treats acne in some people, but also helps minimize the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles, uneven skin tone, and reduces hyperpigmentation by blocking tyrosinase (an enzyme that helps create skin pigment) — benefits that make it transformative for a wider range of people than just those with acute acne concerns.

However, tretinoin’s rise in popularity has divided opinion among skincare experts. “I don’t think tretinoin should have gone viral on TikTok,” says Alicia Lartey, a London-based esthetician. In fact, she feels it is “irresponsible of influencers” in particular (the majority of whom she says have no background in skincare) to promote it. Why? Well, not many people are educating about the downsides, like the fact that this stuff is really strong and, of course, not accessible for everyone.

So here’s the real lowdown on prescription tretinoin — and the best alternative over-the-counter option if you want to avoid a copay.

What is tretinoin?

Tretinoin is topical retinoic acid, a vitamin A derivative that increases skin cell turnover. It’s the most potent topical retinoid (more on that below). It helps to shed dead skin cells and encourage the regrowth of newer, younger skin cells. In that process, it can do a number of things. “Tretinoin helps treat acne, signs of aging, skin texture, and pigmentation,” explains Lartey. It also stimulates collagen synthesis. Consultant dermatologist Dr. Adil Sheraz adds that tretinoin can improve skin elasticity (making it smoother and more plump) and help to achieve an even skin tone.

What’s the difference between tretinoin, retinol, and retinal?

To understand exactly how tretinoin works, it pays to know about the pyramid in which it sits. Dr. Sheraz explains that tretinoin comes from the retinoid family, which includes a number of different forms, all widely available in topical skincare products. In order of potency, it goes: retinoic acid (tretinoin), retinal, retinol, then retinyl palmitate.

Prescription tretinoin sits at the top of the pyramid. “It’s the most potent form of a topical retinoid,” explains Dr. Sheraz. Compared to retinal and retinol, tretinoin is stronger and more active right away, so it works faster. There are several different Rx brands of tretinoin that dermatologists prescribe; Altreno and Retin-A are two of the most popular, but it’s also common to receive the generic version.

Below tretinoin, there’s retinaldehyde, also known as retinal. This ingredient has become increasingly popular over the years and, unlike tretinoin, it’s available over the counter. For example, Peach & Lily, Youth To The People, and Naturium all offer over-the-counter versions of retinal. Without subjecting you to a science lesson, Dr. Sheraz explains that retinal is “converted” in your skin cells so that it becomes active and is able to perform its job. This means that “[retinal] is weaker than tretinoin but stronger than retinol,” explains Dr. Sheraz. Retinal is Lartey’s preferred over-the-counter retinoid. “It also has an antibacterial property,” she says, “which is great for those managing acne.”

Underneath retinal, you’ll find retinol. “This requires multiple conversions in the skin [for it to work] and is significantly weaker than tretinoin,” says Dr. Sheraz. That’s not necessarily a bad thing. “As it’s less potent, it’s less of an irritant, and it can be bought over the counter.”

At the bottom of the retinoid pyramid, you’ll find retinyl palmitate. This is the weakest form of retinoid and often the cheapest as well. Like retinal and retinol, retinyl palmitate is present in OTC skincare, and while it’s less potent and effective, some people prefer it. “Some people get better results using a less effective form because it doesn’t irritate their skin as much, so they’re more likely to use it more often,” cosmetic chemist Randy Schueller of The Beauty Brains told R29.

Put simply, tretinoin is the most powerful of the four, though it’s available at different concentrations, some much stronger than others. “Tretinoin is available in various strengths, both as creams and gels,” explains Dr. Sheraz.

Who is tretinoin good for?

In her NYC practice, Dr. Henry prescribes tretinoin daily to a “wide range” of people. Some people use prescription tretinoin to treat adult-onset acne. “I have some patients who are oily, some who are acne prone,” explains Dr. Henry, “but some [tretinoin patients] don’t have acne at all. I have sensitive-skin patients who still want to derive those benefits who come to me for counsel on how to choose the right tretinoin formulation.”

For people who are using tretinoin for the treatment of fine lines and wrinkles, Dr. Henry says that their skin-care routine may be very simple. “If someone’s coming in for treatment of fine lines and wrinkles, they may just be on tretinoin and moisturizer and sunscreen, and that’s it,” Dr. Henry explains, adding that it’s really a case-by-case conversation. “Some patients on tretinoin are looking for a more sophisticated regimen depending on their skin concerns.”

Where can you get tretinoin?

Don’t buy tretinoin online. You need to see a dermatologist or healthcare provider for a tretinoin prescription. “It’s a prescription because of the strength and the need for someone with more expertise to guide you in using it,” explains Dr. Henry. If you have access to a dermatologist, they will likely be able to prescribe you tretinoin if you’re a good candidate.

In Dr. Henry’s New York practice, she prescribes some form of tretinoin every day. The main reason someone might not be a good candidate is if they can’t tolerate any form of retinol. However, today there are more low-strength tretinoin options. “There are lower concentrations, made with ingredients like ceramides [and] hyaluronic acid, that really make it more tolerable so that it’s an option for more people,” explains Dr. Henry. The lowest prescription concentration of tretinoin is 0.01%, which could be just fine for someone with sensitive skin.

Getting to a dermatologist might not be feasible (which we’ll speak to ahead). Some newer personalized online dermatologist services such as Skin Medicinals and Agency may prescribe tretinoin. However, an extensive digital consultation with a qualified dermatologist will always have to take place first. In some cases, it’s also recommended that you check in with your prescribing dermatologist regularly.

How do you use tretinoin?

This is where you have to be careful. If you see someone on TikTok apply tretinoin like they would a moisturizer, that is wrong and dangerous. According to dermatologists, you only need a pea-sized amount to cover your entire face. Dr. Henry recommends the “sandwich method” of application: “You put moisturizer on first, then your medicine [tretinoin], then more moisturizer.” Use it sparingly and only at night, avoiding sensitive areas, like around your nose, lips, and under eyes. “Start every other night, maybe twice a week, then slowly increase as you tolerate,” explains Dr. Henry.

In terms of the rest of your skin-care routine, Dr. Sheraz recommends that other “active” products be cut out for the time being. This includes any other retinol-based products and acids, as well as benzoyl peroxide.

Dr. Sheraz adds that when you are prescribed tretinoin, your dermatologist or doctor should always check that you have a good understanding of how to properly moisturize your skin. Though this may seem basic, retinoids can make skin feel dry, flaky, and uncomfortable, so getting your moisturizer right is a must. Look for gentle, hydrating, and soothing ingredients such as hyaluronic acid, glycerin, shea butter, and panthenol. Prescribers will also check that you’re using a broad-spectrum sunscreen in the daytime, as retinoids make skin extra sensitive to harmful UV rays.

What are the downsides of using tretinoin?

The biggest downside to tretinoin is, you probably guessed it, skin sensitivity and inflammation. “It can result in significant irritation, redness, peeling, and inflammation in certain individuals,” explains Dr. Sheraz. If you’ve tried OTC retinol in the past and you’re sensitive to it, you can expect to be sensitive if you switch to tretinoin, because it’s even stronger. It’s also important to note that due to its drying effect, tretinoin can occasionally cause eczema flare-ups. “This is why a substantial moisturizer should always be used alongside it,” says Dr. Sheraz. Another disclaimer: Like retinol and retinal, tretinoin can’t be used if you’re pregnant.

Another obvious downside is the cost.

How much does tretinoin cost?

Dr. Henry explains that it’s tricky to generalize cost because it’s an individual insurance equation. “The range could be between zero dollars and $200 depending on the insurance plan, pharmacy insurance copay, and the type of tretinoin,” explains Dr. Henry. Moreover, we have to note that access to a dermatologist is not always possible, which is a barrier to entry with prescriptions like tretinoin.

What are the alternatives to tretinoin?

If you’re looking for what would be the closest alternative to tretinoin that you can get without a prescription, it’s Differin Gel. “Differin is probably one of the most robust options you can find over the counter,” explains Dr. Henry. “That’s what I recommend.” Differin was FDA-approved in 2016 for over-the-counter use. It’s 0.1% adapalene — adapalene is an active form of retinoic acid — which is widely considered a “game changer” in the topical skincare space.

According to the aforementioned pyramid, over-the-counter retinal would also be a good alternative — not as strong as retinoic acid, but stronger and faster than retinol. If you’re super sensitive, Dr. Henry says you could also try an alternative to retinol like bakuchiol, or a serum or cream rich in peptides. “Peptides are similarly going to help stimulate collagen, get rid of fine lines and wrinkles, and help to improve facial scarring,” explains Dr. Henry, who also quotes their side effects as serendipitously good for your skin. Ultimately, trying tretinoin is not a decision to be taken lightly — no matter what TikTok videos might suggest. Thanks to its side effects and potency, it’s always recommended to consult a doctor first and work your way up with other, weaker formulas.
